abstract: |
  Making a motor error, hitting the wrong key for example in responding to a stimulus, impacts perceptual, motor, and cognitive processes by implying a variation in performance and response time on the next trial (Post Error Slowing, Dutilh et al., 2012; Wessel, 2018). Wessel et al. (2022) showed that an error produced on a flanker-type task had a negative impact on a working memory span recognition. This effect is called ERIAM (Error Related Impairment of Active Working Memory) and consists of degradation of memory span following the production of an error on a conflict task concurrent to a memory task. In their study, the ERIAM effect is more pronounced in Low Span individuals. This suggests that these individuals have less stable Working Memory representations and are more likely to be impacted by an error. The presented study replicates the ERIAM protocol of Wessel et al. (2022) by adding variation of cognitive load. In addition, span recognition task is modified with a recall task. Results show a replication of ERIAM effect in our sample. Morever, ERIAM effect is only significant in lowspan group in the moderate cognitive load condition and in highspan group in the increased load condition. In line with Lavie's load theory (Lavie et al., 2004), we explain these results by the fact that High and Low Span groups do not process cognitive load increase in the same way.

keywords: [Working Memory, Error, Cognitive load, Error Related Impairment of Active Working Memory, Conflict Tasks]

# Introduction

The examination of post-error phenomena has been an ongoing endeavour since the 1960s (Danielmeier & Ullsperger, 2011; Dudschig & Jentzsch, 2009; Dutilh et al., 2012; Laming, 1979; Notebaert et al., 2009; Pfister & Foerster, 2021) and the publication of Rabbitt's article. (Rabbitt, 1966). Since the inception of the field, studies have been predicated on the observation of behavioural phenomena arising in the aftermath of errors. Such phenomena include the lengthening of response times (RTs) and the subsequent modification of accuracy. These behavioural adjustments have been designated Post-Error Adjustments (PEA) (Danielmeier & Ullsperger, 2011), and are a means to infer underlying cognitive processes. PEA has been linked to cognitive control and working memory implementation (Regev & Meiran, 2014). The presence of PEA has been documented in a variety of conflict tasks, including the flanker task (Debener et al., 2005), Stroop task (Gehring & Fencsik, 2001), and Simon task (King et al., 2010). In a dual-task procedure intertwined with a working memory span task, J. Wessel and Jiang (2021a) collected data showing the impact of a motor error on working memory maintenance. This study experimentally linked error to higher-order cognitive functions (working memory, cognitive control and attention).
In order to discuss error, it is essential to consider the Error Generic Error Modelling System (GEMS), which was developed by Reason (Reason, 1990). GEMS provides a robust foundation for the classification of errors according to the levels of processing achieved. The system categorises errors into three distinct categories: skill-based errors, rule-based errors, and knowledge-based errors. In this study, our primary focus is on the initial level, designated as 'skill-based' (see Skill-Rule-Knowledge (Rasmussen, 1983), from which Reason's model is derived). This level encompasses errors attributable to a lack of attention or to habitual responses. These errors are associated with an absence of attention to the pertinent aspects of the information to be processed. These errors can also be attributed to irrelevant aspects of the task or stimulus, as evidenced in conflict tasks, where attention is diverted from the task's objectives. Cognitive systems have been shown to monitor these errors (Botvinick et al., 2001), and to facilitate the detection and correction of errors through the engagement of cognitive control.
In accordance with the seminal work of Miyake et al. (2000), cognitive control is delineated as a triad of factors: the inhibition of a prepotent response, the updating of working memory, and the shifting between mental sets. These factors exhibit distinct variance and correlations, as elucidated by Friedman and Robbins (2022). The occurrence of cognitive control is immediate upon the detection of an error (Shalgi et al., 2009), with the purpose of monitoring such errors (Botvinick et al., 2004). As demonstrated by Unsworth et al. (2022), High Span individuals (who possess superior working memory capacities: WMC) exhibit a reduced propensity to encounter attentional fluctuations during task execution. These individuals demonstrate an enhanced capacity to oversee errors (i.e., error monitoring). Conversely, Low Span individuals have been observed to demonstrate a propensity for unperceived errors, also termed error blindness (Buzzell et al., 2017), which is attributable to attentional fluctuations or mind wandering (Christoff et al., 2016). Cognitive control has been demonstrated to play a role in the ability to manage perceived errors and is related to attention. In order to detect an error, individuals must remain in a sufficient alert state, which is expensive in terms of attentional resources. Error awareness has been shown to be negatively correlated with attentional deficits and positively correlated with working memory capacities (WMC). As posited by Botvinick et al. (2001), the cognitive system is responsible for evaluating the necessity for cognitive control by identifying the occurrence of conflict in information processing. In the event of an error, this system activates (Botvinick et al., 2004), with the objective of resolving the conflict generated by the discrepancy between the formulated response and the anticipated response. Upon resolution of the conflict, the individual is able to redirect their focus to the task at hand, thereby mobilising all cognitive and attentional resources to achieve their objectives. The monitoring of errors and the subsequent adjustments in behaviour that occur in response to errors have been shown to provide insight into the underlying attentional and cognitive processes (Botvinick et al., 2004). It has been demonstrated to be informative of lapses of attention (Unsworth et al., 2022) and cognitive control (Regev & Meiran, 2014). According to Engle and Kane (2003), a robust correlation exists between WMC, attentional control, and the conflict management system. Improved WMC has been shown to facilitate enhanced conflict detection and more effective implementation of attentional control (Unsworth et al., 2022). Consequently, individuals with superior WMC (and thus superior attentional control) are likely to demonstrate enhanced efficacy in processing errors (Unsworth et al., 2022).
“Everyone knows what attention is. It is the taking possession by the mind, in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought.” (James, 1890). Attention is crucial in processing information. As Egeth & Kahneman (1975) and Wickens (2008) models postulate, the limited capacity of human information processing capabilities is dependent on the limited capacity of the human reservoir of attention. The selection of relevant information is therefore a prerequisite for achieving the goals of the individual (Niedermeyer, 1994). Selectivity is defined as the distinction between two distinct functions of attention: the first being divided attention, which implies that attention is considered a reserve of processing resources; and the second being selective attention, which implies that attention is an instance of conscious control of processing. The hypothesis that perception has limited capacities was first put forward at the perceptual level ( BROADBENT, 1958; TREISMAN, 1964). Subsequently, the hypothesis of a later selection (Deutsch & Deutsch, 1963) was formulated, proposing the perception of stimuli as an automatic process. Lavie and Dalton (2014) finally proposed a hybrid model that allows for both types of selection.
In order to achieve the selection of information, it is first necessary to exercise control over one's attention. Attentional control can be defined as the ability to focus and maintain attentional resources on a specific task or goal, while discarding information (e.g. from thoughts or external stimuli) that is not relevant to that goal. Attentional resources are oriented endogenously (i.e. top-down), according to the individual's goals and objectives, by attentional control (i.e. executive attention). These resources are then directed in a controlled and voluntary manner to the relevant aspects of the environment and/or internal cognitive processes for the achievement of these goals. The prefrontal cortex (particularly the dorsolateral area) supports the active maintenance of the goals in progress in the task and has been linked to the WMC of individuals (Kane & Engle, 2002). In order to understand the factors that affect the process of selecting relevant information, Lavie proposed a theory that measures the impact of two types of load: perceptual and cognitive loads.
Lavie and Tsal (Lavie & Tsal, 1994) propose perceptual load theory (see also Lavie & Dalton, 2014 and Lavie, 2010), which models selective attention and resolves the debate about the location of attentional filtering. According to this theory, the primary determinant of the locus of attentional filtering is perceptual load. In their protocol, Forster & Lavie (2007) propose a task for participants to detect the presence of a target letter among two pre-specified possibilities (e.g. X or N) in a circle composed of items. In the experiment, a distractor letter is displayed adjacent to the circle. This distractor letter corresponds either to the target letter (in what is termed the 'congruent condition', e.g. target "X" and distractor letter "X") or to the other alternative (in what is termed the 'incongruent condition', e.g. target "X" and distractor letter "N"). The effect of the distractor letter is measured by the difference in response time to the target between the congruent and incongruent conditions. In incongruent trials, where the distractor letter is an alternative to the target, response times are observed to increase. In the low-load condition, the circle is composed of small "o"s and the target letter, thus accentuating the target letter within the circle (Posner, 1980). Conversely, in the high load condition, the circle is composed of other letters along with the target letter. The authors of the study observed that in the high perceptual load condition (where the circle is composed of other letters), the effect of the distractor letter on response time is almost entirely cancelled. This suggests that a higher perceptual load may serve to either decrease or even cancel the effects of distractors, and in this particular instance, an early attentional filtering process limits the perception of irrelevant elements.
In circumstances where the perceptual load is minimal, individuals' residual processing abilities may be influenced by irrelevant distractor stimuli. This suggests the necessity for subsequent selection processes to be implemented in order to prevent these distractors from exerting control over behaviour (Lavie, 2010). Lavie and Dalton (2014) proposed a dual-task protocol to measure the effect of cognitive load on distractor processing. The protocol entailed the administration of a memory task, in which participants were required to memorise a digit span, followed by a selective attention task, prior to the presentation of the digit span at baseline. In the context of the selective attention task, participants are instructed to identify a central target letter (z or x) presented concurrently with a peripheral distractor letter that is either congruent, incongruent, or neutral. This configuration results in a minimal perceptual load, consisting solely of the target letter and the distractor letter. In the digit span task, the number of digits presented is varied (from 1 to 6) to observe the effect of cognitive load on distractor processing. It is hypothesised that a higher cognitive load will increase the effect of the distractor on response time, which is the opposite effect to that of a higher perceptual load.
Should the presentation of the stimulus engender a high level of perceptual load, then attentional filtering will be early and automatic, resulting in the individual's perceptual limits being reached. Distractors that are not relevant to the task at hand may not even be perceived. However, should this level allow for all perceived information (both relevant and irrelevant) to be processed without overload, filtering will occur at the higher (cognitive) level of processing. The consequences of this filtering process depend on its location. In cases where filtering occurs early, it leads to minimized distractibility to irrelevant stimuli due to these stimuli being filtered and, consequently, not perceived. Conversely, a low perceptual load has been shown to result in an increased susceptibility to irrelevant stimuli. Furthermore, an elevated cognitive load has been demonstrated to exacerbate the impact of distractors. The effects of perceptual and cognitive load on the processing of distractors, such as task-irrelevant stimuli, are contradictory. The present study will concentrate on the cognitive load effect on attentional processes.
The observed differences in WMC between the high and low span groups can be attributed to variations in attentional control. In order to ascertain the methodologies employed by diverse participant groups in the effective selection of pertinent information while filtering out irrelevant data, Kane & Engle (Kane & Engle, 2000) conducted an evaluation of the performance of two participant cohorts distinguished by their WMC (high span vs. low span). The experiment involved the presentation of a list of words. During the encoding phase, participants are required to tap a simple sequence on a keyboard in accordance with a predetermined rhythm. This is followed by an interfering task (oral version of the Trail Making Test (Armitage, 1946), which lasts for 16 seconds in order to prevent participants from repeating the list. Participants are then asked to recall the list. Initial trials revealed that Low Spans demonstrated equivalent performance to High Spans. However, subsequent trials indicated that High Span participants exhibited superior performance in comparison to Low Span participants. This phenomenon can be attributed to the proactive interference inhibition exhibited by High Span participants. Their superior attentional control capacity enables them to effectively counteract the effects of interference, thereby ensuring enhanced recall efficacy in the presence of interference.
The authors then propose an increase in the complexity of the sequence in which participants type with their finger following the encoding of the word list. This results in an overall cognitive cost to the task that increases, thus making the procedure more similar to a dual task. In this case, the authors no longer observe a greater effect of proactive interference in Low Span compared to High Span. They conclude that High Span participants are no longer able to counteract the effects of proactive interference in situations of higher cognitive load. Attentional control is a voluntary and resource-intensive process. As cognitive load increases, conflict resolution (proactive interference) is impaired in High Span participants because they are no longer able to deploy sufficient attentional resources. This has a subsequent impact on recall of the word list. In Low Span, attentional control is not used to counteract the effects of proactive interference, and this results in a stronger effect of this interference (than in High Span) and no difference between load conditions.
In order to assess behavioural responses to errors, conflict tasks (e.g. flanker task, Simon task, Stroop task) are frequently employed in laboratory settings (Derrfuss et al., 2021; Schroder et al., 2019; Steinhauser et al., 2017). These tasks are also commonly utilised to demonstrate attentional control (Bastian et al., 2020) implementation. The design of these tasks requires participants to select one option from a series of alternatives as expeditiously as possible. The complexity of these tasks stems from the strategic manipulation of the relevant and irrelevant dimensions of the presented stimuli. Congruence is characterised by the similarity between the information provided by the target (relevant) and the distractors (irrelevant).In contrast, incongruence is defined by the divergence between these two dimensions. In congruent trials, participants typically exhibit a higher level of accuracy and faster response times compared to incongruent trials (EGNER, 2007). The incongruent condition involves the interference of information from two distinct dimensions, leading to a conflict in response selection and the subsequent activation of the conflict management system. Incongruent trials have been shown to be more prone to generating errors (Gratton et al., 2017). Consequently, conflict tasks have been shown to induce errors in participants.
In the domain of error behavioural adjustments, Post-Error Slowing (PES) is defined as an increase in reaction time (RT) on post-error trials (Laming, 1979). Conversely, Post-Improvement of Accuracy (PIA) is characterised by an enhancement in response accuracy on post-error trials. The relationship between response time and response accuracy on post-error trials is associated with the emergence of two predominant theoretical frameworks: The former, termed functional theories of PES (Fievez et al., 2022), are predicated on observations of enhanced accuracy levels in response to post-error trials, while the latter, termed non-functional theories of PES, posit a decrease of accuracy in post-error trials. PIA is not uniformly substantiated in the extant scientific literature. The extant literature on the subject is inconclusive, with some studies reporting a link between PES and PIA (e.g., Maier et al., 2011; Marco-Pallarés et al., 2008) while others not (e.g., Carp & Compton, 2009; Fiehler et al., 2005). These theories are also referred to as adaptive (functional) and maladaptive (non-functional). The improvement in post-error accuracy has been demonstrated to support the functional/adaptive explanations for PES. The stream of adaptive theories provides a functional value to PES. In conjunction with the concomitant observation of increased accuracy on trials following the error (PIA; Danielmeier et al., 2011), PES enables participants to regain an optimal level of performance on the task. The link between subsequent increase in accuracy and PES has been modeled in a Drift Diffusion type computational model (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008). This model shows a post-error increase in response caution materialized by a decrease in drift rate (Dutilh et al., 2011). The drift rate is parameter of the model that represents how quickly informations from the stimulus are collected. According to Dutilh et al. (2012), “[…] participants become more cautious after an error and slightly more daring after a correct response […]”.
Conversely, in instances where post-error accuracy does not demonstrate an increase (Schroder et al., 2019), non-functional/maladaptive theories offer a more suitable explanation for PES. Maladaptive theories propose that PES emerges as a diversion of attention to irrelevant aspects of the task at hand. Error is defined as an unexpected event for the participant, thereby directing their attention towards it. However, when the task becomes more challenging and errors begin to outnumber correct responses, a phenomenon referred to as the Post-Correct Slowing effect is observed (Notebaert et al., 2009). This effect involves an increase in reaction times (RTs) following a correct response, which is the opposite of the PES. Here it’s the unexpected aspect that causes the slowdown, and depending on the relative frequency of the stimuli, it can be either an error trial or a correct trial. In their protocol, errors are not followed by an improvement of subsequent performance (PIA). PES therefore has no functional value. Other theories in this current (maladaptive theory) postulate an impossibility to process the additional information constituted by error. These theories propose that the processing of additional information, such as errors, is impeded by a bottleneck in the information processing capacity, resulting in a saturation of ongoing cognitive processes. By manipulating the response/stimulus interval, Jentzsch and Dudschig (2009) observed that the shortest intervals (50 ms) resulted in the highest PES, which was associated with a decline in response accuracy. Over the longest intervals (1000 ms), the authors report a reduction in PES compared to the shortest intervals and no significant variation of response accuracy.
Subsequent research has enabled the convergence of divergent data patterns from adaptive and maladaptive theories. J. R. Wessel (2017) synthesises these contradictory approaches and demonstrates their complementarity with Adaptive Orienting Theory (AOT). This theory postulates that PES is a phenomenon that occurs in two phases. Initially, there is a broad inhibition of perceptual, motor and cognitive processes that are activated to carry out the task. Attention is diverted from the goals of the task by the surprise effect caused by an error, but this phenomenon is not error-specific, and any unexpected event is likely to provoke this pattern. This leads to a decrease in accuracy and an increase in RTs. Wessel speaks of 'orienting-related' PES, and the next stimulus arrives too early during the inhibition period of PES. Consequently, the occurrence of PIA is not observed, thereby facilitating the consideration of data derived from non-functional (maladaptive) theories. 
In the subsequent stage, J. R. Wessel (2017) delineates an error-specific phase in which the source of attentional disturbance is identified and examined. During this phase, attentional processes aimed at processing errors are progressively reallocated. In this phase, attention is oriented towards errors to facilitate their processing. This is followed by a reengagement with the goals of the current task and a restoration of pre-error performance levels. The purpose of this subsequent phase is to facilitate the restoration of optimal levels of accuracy in the task at hand. PES is then described as 'strategic', a deliberate and gradual process influenced by cognitive control. Once these two stages have been completed, PIA can be observed, as postulated by adaptive theories. PES has a functional status by allowing the refocusing of attentional processes on the current task to recover pre-error performance levels.
In their seminal work, J. Wessel and Jiang (2021a) sought to establish a correlation between motor error, working memory (WM) processes, and attentional processes. To this end, they proposed a protocol to test one of the predictions of Adaptive Orienting Theory (J. R. Wessel, 2017). This protocol sought to ascertain the impact of a motor error on ongoing cognitive processes during the task. The experimental protocol employed is a dual-task protocol (see Box 1), comprising a memory task and a flanker task (Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974). The trial sequence is outlined as follows: Initially, a series of letters is displayed on the screen for a duration of 2000 milliseconds, requiring memory retention. Participants are then required to indicate the direction of a central arrow (the target, indicating left or right) while ignoring two distractor arrows symmetrically arranged to the left and right of this target. The distractor arrows both point in the same direction as the target (congruent trial) or in the opposite direction (incongruent trial). Following the completion of six trials of the arrow task, a series of letters is again presented to the participants. In 50% of cases, the series exhibited a correspondence with the series presented at the commencement of the trial. Participants were tasked with evaluating the congruence between the two sets of letters through a YES/NO response. Prior to the initiation of the protocol, a training phase is employed to calibrate the size of the series of letters presented to the participants' abilities. Thereafter, the set undergoes an increase or decrease of one item, contingent on the participants' recognition responses. Trial categorization as either a correct or an error trial is contingent upon the occurrence of an error during the arrow task.
The authors of the study observed that error trials resulted in a decrease in the level of accuracy on the recognition of the span in comparison to correct trials, which is known as the ERIAM effect (Error Related Impairment of Active Working Memory). In Experiment 2, the ERIAM effect demonstrated a medium effect size (t(52) = 3.29, p = .002, Cohen's d = .45). However, no increase in response times on span recognition was observed, which would then more specifically signify a speed-accuracy trade-off (SAT) adjustment (Donkin et al., 2014). A decrease in the accuracy of working memory recall, which is associated with a decrease in response times, can be more simply explained by a decrease in the time taken by subjects to formulate and provide the correct response. Furthermore, the authors increased the inter-stimulus interval (from 200 to 2300 milliseconds in Experiment 1 and Experiment 2, respectively) and once again obtained an ERIAM effect with a longer interval. This finding demonstrates that the ERIAM effect is not contingent on the bottleneck passage of information postulated by some non-functional theories of PES (Jentzsch & Dudschig, 2009). The ERIAM effect is more pronounced in Low Span participants than in High Span participants, thereby providing a link between WM capacities and error monitoring abilities (Unsworth et al., 2022).


> **Box 1:** McIsaac et al. (2015) proposes a taxonomy of dual-task paradigms. A dual task is the concurrent performance of two tasks that can be performed separately, measured separately, and have distinct goals. Thus, each task may be different in character, drawing on distinct domains. For example, a memorization task will be based on mnemonic and cognitive processes. Another task may consist of performing a movement. The two tasks may also be based partly or totally on similar processes. (two tasks of a cognitive nature). In J. Wessel and jiang (2021a) , the protocol implemented involves a memory task and a motor task of deciding the direction of an arrow. The motor task requires selective attentional abilities, as it involves not being disturbed by distracting arrows of a flanker-type task (Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974). The memory task proposed by J. Wessel and jiang (2021a) , taken independently, is a simple short-term memory task. Participants are asked to recognize a letter span presented a few seconds earlier. It is the performance of this task in a dual-task protocol that makes it a Working Memory task.*

The study conducted by J. Wessel and jiang (2021a) , while offering interesting results, can be subject to a few limitations, particularly on the methodological level. One limitation, due to post-hoc hypothesizing of a link between the ERIAM effect and WM capacities, is impossible experimental control of claim. In fact, over the course of five experiments in their study, Wessel and colleagues observed a negative correlation between ERIAM effect and participants’ WM capacities (r = -.41, p < .001). High Span individuals are less impacted by motor error than are Low Span individuals. One experiment in the protocol proposes to increase the number of items in the memory span. Similar in all respects to the previous experiment, the authors no longer observed a significant correlation between the ERIAM effect and WM capacities when the cognitive load was increased (r = -.37, p = .071). This observation needs further exploration and this work attempts to address it by systematically varying the number of items to be memorized and by performing linear regression analyses.
The present study will observe the effects of an error on a digit span in working memory by implementing a complex span protocol. This type of protocol (reading span [Daneman & Carpenter, 1980]; operation span [Turner & Engle, 1989]; symmetry span [Kane et al., 2004]) requires participants to maintain items in memory while performing a second concurrent task. The maintenance of working memory and the selection of salient aspects of the stimuli within the same task are both called upon. The error on the conflict task will then allow for the categorisation of trials according to their accuracy and for the estimation of the effect of the error on the maintenance of the working memory span.
The primary objective of this study is to replicate the ERIAM effect (J. Wessel & Jiang, 2021a) by implementing a modified version of Experiment 2, where the most significant ERIAM effect was observed. Trials are conducted in a laboratory setting to ensure the collection of the most precise data, unencumbered by the constraints of online runs related to connections and/or hardware. The objective is twofold: firstly, to provide new data to retest the finding of J. Wessel and Jiang (2021a); and secondly, to attempt to verify Adaptive Orienting Theory's (J. R. Wessel, 2017) prediction of error-induced inhibition of ongoing cognitive processes during the task. The WM task is to be closed with digit span recall rather than recognition, as we propose. This approach is underpinned by the observation that the recognition response to the WM task engages the same response modalities as the conflict task, both of which involve choosing between two possibilities: YES/NO for the similarity to the set of digits and Left/Right for the direction of the target arrow on the arrow task. The use of the numeric keypad keys to recall the digit span facilitates the dissociation of these response modalities and the observation of performance on the WM task by minimising the confusion of response modalities (Pashler, 1990).
Furthermore, J. Wessel and Jiang (2021a) demonstrated a significant negative correlation (in five out of seven experiments) between the ERIAM effect and subjects' average WMC, concluding that the ERIAM effect more strongly impacts subjects for whom the memory task is more demanding. Individuals with better WMC are those who are better able to regulate their attentional processes and to monitor the occurrence of error. The ERIAM effect appears to be less pronounced for individuals with higher working memory capacity (WMC) compared to those with lower WMC. However, a notable point that merits attention is the observation that the correlation between the ERIAM effect and WMC becomes marginal and non-significant when an increase in cognitive load is introduced, as evidenced by the transition from Experiment 5 to Experiment 6. This decline in the ERIAM/WMC correlation with increasing cognitive load is a subject that merits further investigation, particularly given that the two experiments that led to this difference in results involved two separate samples.


## Presentation of hypotheses

We expect to observe a degradation in memory recall performance following a motor error (i.e., on flanker task). **This constitutes our first hypothesis.** We will replicate, using a slightly modified task, the ERIAM effect observed by @wessel2021 .

During an increase in cognitive load, High Span subjects will have their attentional resources mobilized more extensively on the recall of the span and will have less ability to inhibit the effect of an error on motor task. Low Span subjects will be less affected by the increase in cognitive load because their attentional resources will have already been consumed at lower levels of load. **This constitutes our second hypothesis.** We will test ERIAM effect in these two groups and under these two conditions of cognitive load.

Following our second hypothesis testing we propose **an exploratory part** (with analysis made post-hoc after hypothesis 2 testing) to try to increase our understanding of ERIAM effect. In this part we test more low-level construct (accuracy) within group span and cognitive load condition.

Then, we will observe the ERIAM/WMC correlation. We will observe this correlation in both groups and condition of load. @kane2000 showed that High Span individuals were more impacted by an increase in cognitive load than Low Span individuals. @thomassin2015 also found a similar pattern in their study, High Span individuals' strategies are more efficient but also more sensitive to task's complexity. This effect was named *Hard Fall Effect*. We propose that correlation between ERIAM and WMC will become positive in high span group as cognitive load increase. In low span group we expect not to see such a difference between load condition. **This constitutes our third hypothesis**.

Finally, a **second exploratory part** is proposed with post-hoc analysis following hypothesis 3. Without taking care of cognitive load, we want to observe ERIAM/WMC for the whole group (as Wessel et al. did in their study), and in the high and low span groups.

## Methods

### Participants / Sample size justification

We choose to take part of information we have to justify our sample size. Original study want to reach a 80% power collecting data on 53 participants. To ensure good probabilities of replication, we increase our a priori power to 90% [@erdfelder1996]. Data on a sample of `r max(combined_data$Subject)` participants were collected. The participants gave their free and informed consent to undergo the experiment. Research Ethics Committee of Toulouse accepted the research by ruling on the ethical compliance of the present study (2023-596). The study was pre-registered on OSF [@brochet2022]. The final sample consisted of 58 participants after data processing (as 5 participants did not fulfill the whole experiment) with `r round(table(combined_data$Sex)["femme"] / length(combined_data$Sex) * 100, 2)`% women and `r round(table(combined_data$Sex)["homme"] / length(combined_data$Sex) * 100, 2)`% men (age: *M* = `r round(mean(combined_data$Age),2)`, *SD* = `r round(sd(combined_data$Age),2)`).

### Material/Stimuli

Stimuli for conflict task (the target arrow and the four winged arrows surrounding it) were composed of a five-character string with symbols "\>" and "\<" . Width and height of stimuli represent 10.8° and 3.3° of visual angle, respectively (centered on a 17-inch screen located 60 centimeters from participants. Stimulus for flanker task consists of target and four flankers distributed two by two on each side of target (e.g. \>\>\<\>\>). For memory task, digits from 0 to 9 are presented in *Times New Roman* font size 80. Each digit in series is separated from the other digits by the '-' character to limit deliberate chunking [@gobet2012]. Series of digits are constructed in random mode, with possible repetition (to make series larger than 10 digits possible). All stimuli are displayed in white on a black background. The task was programmed on Eprime 3.0 software (Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA).

### Procedure

Structure of the task is shown in **Figure 1**. Each trial is structured in the same way. Trial begins with presentation of a fixation cross centered on screen for 1,000 ms, followed by presentation of series of digits at the same location on screen for 2000 ms. A neutral screen (black screen) is then presented for 200 ms before the start of flanker task. Flanker task consists of a sequence of four stimuli for a total duration of 4800 ms. Stimulus consists of target accompanied by 4 flankers, presented on screen for 200 ms. Each stimulus is followed by a black screen for 1000ms allowing participants to respond. We did not proceed to a priming unlike the replicated study (100 ms of advance for flankers, then addition of target for 100 ms). The 4 flankers all pointed in the same direction (left or right) and depending on whether central target pointed in direction of the flankers or the opposite direction, the trial was considered congruent or incongruent, respectively. Participants were asked to respond to the orientation of the central target regardless of the flankers as quickly as possible by pressing the "A" or "P" keys for left and right, respectively. The 4 stimuli of flanker task are followed by the number series recall task. Participants are then instructed to recall serie presented to them at beginning of trial using number pad and then validate with ENTER. There is no time limit defined on this recall task, next trial is presented only after participants have validated.

**Figure 1: Task procedure** ![Task procedure](illustration%20tâche.png){fig-align="left" width="500"}

### Training trials for span calibration

Experiment consists of two parts. First part consists of a training of 24 trials during which length of the span varies according to participant's response accuracy. Objective is to calibrate length of the series requested in memory task to subjects' capacities. Span could thus increase by one, remain stable or decrease by one digit depending on participants' two previous answers accuracy (for two correct answers, one correct answer or zero correct answer respectively). Initial span is set on four digits. Participants were not aware of the purpose of these calibration trials. This calibration portion consists only of congruent flanker stimuli so that:

-   Participants could become familiar with structure of the trials and response modalities.

-   Digit span recall is not overly impacted by motor errors in calibration phase.

On this training phase, after each of the participants' actions, feedback is given (green dot for good response, red dot for bad response or "not fast enough" on flanker task if participants do not respond fast enough, response to digit span is not time limited). No participant achieved a memory digit span of less than four digits.

### Completion of the task

Second part consists of the task itself, composed of 60 memory trials. Flanker stimuli are congruent and incongruent (same proportion of 50-50%) within each memory trial. In order to test our second hypothesis, an increase in digit span is performed adding one digit to the set calibrated in the training phase, on half of the trials. Total duration of the experiment is approximately 20 minutes.

### Data analysis

We proceeded to analyze the behavioral data (accuracy and RT) from portion of task without training/calibration trials. We remove trials where participants did not respond on flanker task or memory task. Trials where response on flanker task was less than 200ms were also deleted. Data from memory span responses were, as in replicated study, transformed into proportion of correct responses to conduct analyses. Analyses are between-subjects, data were agglomerated between participants, allowing to invoke central limit theorem.

To test our first hypothesis we compared digit span response accuracy between error and correct conditions (depending on whether an error was produced on interfering flanker task) by two-sided paired-samples T-test at .029 alpha threshold corrected for two-stage study [@pocock1977]. In these two conditions level of congruence is similar (of 50%) in order not to confuse ERIAM effect with a congruence effect.

In order to test our second hypothesis of greater impact of an increase in cognitive load in high span participants on ERIAM effect, we fitted a linear mixed model (estimated using restricted maximum likelihood) to predict ERIAM effect with cognitive load (CL) and High/Low span group (formula: ERIAM \~ CL \* span + (1 \| Subject) ). Groups are differentiated by number of digits in digit span (above and below the sample median). Cognitive load levels differ by adding one item in the digit span (for the increased load condition) compared to the moderate condition. ERIAM effect is calculated as the difference in Working Memory recall accuracies between error and correct conditions on conflict task.

Next, we also reported correlation between ERIAM effect and WMC for comparison with the replicated study. WMC are operationalized as overall digit span average response accuracy without taking into account error and correct conditions on the flanker task. We then observed this correlation in the High span and Low span group and under both conditions of cognitive load. Regression analyses were conducted to test for significance, with participants' WMC as predictors of the ERIAM effect.

# Results

We conducted a interim data analysis on this study (at *N*/2 in april 2023). To preserve the significance of our hypothesis tests, we chose to apply a Pocock correction [@pocock1977] to the alpha thresholds of our primary hypotheses. Employing a two-stage design with two looks at the data, the Pocock correction indicates an alpha level of **0.029** for two-tailed tests. Consequently, we apply this alpha level throughout the remainder of the study. Summary statistics is available in **Table 1**.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# data filtering without RT<200ms
base4 <- filter(combined_data, Slide3.RT >= 200)

# Mean and SD
base5 <- base4 %>%
  group_by(Subject) %>%
  summarize(
    Mean_Mem_erreur = mean(Mem_erreur, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean_Mem_correct = mean(Mem_correct, na.rm = TRUE),
    TR_Mem_Correct = mean(ifelse(erreur_flanker == 1, NA, CollectResponse1.RT), na.rm = TRUE),
    TR_Mem_Erreur = mean(ifelse(erreur_flanker == 0, NA, CollectResponse1.RT), na.rm = TRUE),
    SD_Mem_erreur = sd(Mem_erreur, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD_Mem_correct = sd(Mem_correct, na.rm = TRUE),
    delta_mean = sum(Mean_Mem_correct - Mean_Mem_erreur),
    WMC = mean(CollectResponse1.ACC, na.rm = TRUE),
    NDigit = mean(Ndigit, na.rm = TRUE),
    TRFlankerINC = mean(ifelse(ItemFlanker == 1, NA, Slide3.RT / 1000), na.rm = TRUE),
    TRFlankerCON = mean(ifelse(ItemFlanker == 0, NA, Slide3.RT / 1000), na.rm = TRUE),
    Flanker.AccINC = mean(ifelse(ItemFlanker == 1, NA, Slide3.ACC), na.rm = TRUE),
    Flanker.AccCON = mean(ifelse(ItemFlanker == 0, NA, Slide3.ACC), na.rm = TRUE),
    Flanker.Acc = mean(Slide3.ACC, na.rm = TRUE),
    TRFlanker = mean(Slide3.RT, na.rm = TRUE)/1000
  ) %>% 
  ungroup()

# Effectuer le test t de Student pour précision
result <- t.test(base5$Flanker.AccCON, base5$Flanker.AccINC, paired=TRUE)

# Extraire les résultats du test
dfcon <- result$parameter  # Degrés de liberté
t_valuecon <- result$statistic  # Valeur t
p_valuecon <- result$p.value #pvalue

# Calculer le coefficient de Cohen (Cohen's d)
cohen_d<-cohens_d(t.test(base5$Flanker.AccCON, base5$Flanker.AccINC, paired=TRUE)) %>% 
  select("Cohens_d") %>% 
  round(2)

# Effectuer le test t de Student pour temps de réponse
result2 <- t.test(base5$TRFlankerCON, base5$TRFlankerINC, paired=TRUE)

# Extraire les résultats du test
dfcon2 <- result2$parameter  # Degrés de liberté
t_valuecon2 <- result2$statistic  # Valeur t
p_valuecon2 <- result2$p.value

# Calculer le coefficient de Cohen (Cohen's d)
cohen_d2<-cohens_d(t.test(base5$TRFlankerCON, base5$TRFlankerINC, paired=TRUE)) %>% 
  select("Cohens_d") %>%
  rename("Cohens_d2"="Cohens_d")
  round(2)

base5 <- na.omit(base5)
# Enregistrer les données
write.csv(base5, file = "traitement/analyse R/moyenne_ET_sujetnew.csv")
```

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
means <- c(
  mean(dataa$"Accuracy/error_trial", na.rm = TRUE),
  mean(dataa$"Accuracy/correct_trial", na.rm = TRUE),
  mean(dataa$"RT/error_trial", na.rm = TRUE),
  mean(dataa$"RT/correct_trial", na.rm = TRUE)
)

sds <- c(
  sd(dataa$"Accuracy/error_trial", na.rm = TRUE),
  sd(dataa$"Accuracy/correct_trial", na.rm = TRUE),
  sd(dataa$"RT/error_trial", na.rm = TRUE),
  sd(dataa$"RT/correct_trial", na.rm = TRUE)
)

ci <- function(x) {
  se <- sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(x)))
  mean_val <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  lower <- mean_val - (1.96 * se)  # Interval de confiance à 95%
  upper <- mean_val + (1.96 * se)  # Interval de confiance à 95%
  paste0(format(mean_val, digits = 2), " (", format(sd(x, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 2), ") [", format(lower, digits = 2), " : ", format(upper, digits = 2), "]")
}

means_ci <- sapply(dataa, ci)

data_conflict <- data.frame(
  "RT/congruent_trial" = base7$TRFlankerCON,
  "RT/incongruent_trial" = base7$TRFlankerINC,
  "Accuracy/congruent_trial" = base7$Flanker.AccCON,
  "Accuracy/incongruent_trial" = base7$Flanker.AccINC
)

sds_conflict <- sapply(data_conflict, sd, na.rm = TRUE)
means_ci_conflict <- sapply(data_conflict, ci)

table_data <- data.frame(
  Task = c("WORKING MEMORY", rep("", 3), "------------", "FLANKER", rep("", 3)),
  Mean_SE_CI = c(means_ci[1:4], "", means_ci_conflict[1:4])
)

# Inversion de l'ordre des colonnes
table_data <- table_data[, c("Task", "Mean_SE_CI")]

# Correction des annotations de la colonne Mean_SE_CI
table_data$Mean_SE_CI <- gsub("\\[", "[", table_data$Mean_SE_CI)
table_data$Mean_SE_CI <- gsub("\\]", "]", table_data$Mean_SE_CI)

apa_table(table_data, caption = "Summary of descriptive statistics on each task of the protocol", placement = "H", landscape = FALSE, note = "For each task of the protocol, Mean, Standard Error (SE), and 95% Confidence Interval [CI] are represented. For the Working Memory task, accuracy and response time (RT in second) are represented according to error or correct trial on Conflict Task. For flanker task, RT and accuracy are represented according to congruent or incongruent trials.")
```

## Hypothesis 1 testing

### Conflict task results

An illustration of the results observed on the conflict task is offered in **Figure 2 (a&b),** summary statistics is available in **Table 1**. Compared to congruent trials, incongruent trials were less accurate (*t*(`r dfcon`) = `r round(t_valuecon,2)`, *p*`r format_p(p_valuecon)`, Cohen's *d* = `r round(cohen_d$Cohens_d,2)`) and had longer RTs than congruent trials (*t*(`r dfcon2`) = `r round(t_valuecon2,2)`, *p*`r format_p(p_valuecon2)`, Cohen's *d* = `r abs(round(cohen_d2$Cohens_d2, 2))`). This indicates that the manipulation in the conflict task worked by replicating the conflict interference effects widely documented in the literature.

**Figure 2: Accuracy and Response Time on conflict task**

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# create a dataset
base6 <- read_csv("traitement/analyse R/moyenne_ET_sujetnew.csv")

base8 <- subset(base6, select = -c(Flanker.Acc, TRFlanker))
base8 <- base8 %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("Flanker.Acc"), names_to = "Condition", values_to = "Accuracy") %>%
  mutate(Condition = ifelse(Condition == "Flanker.AccCON", "Congruent", "Incongruent"))

base9 <- subset(base6, select = -c(Flanker.Acc, TRFlanker)) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("TRFlanker"), names_to = "Condition", values_to = "TRFlanker") %>%
  mutate(Condition = ifelse(Condition == "TRFlankerCON", "Congruent", "Incongruent"), TRFlanker = TRFlanker*1000)
```

### Memory task results

An illustration of the observed results is shown in **Figure 3(a&b),** summary statistics is available in **Table 1**. The participants' memory load consisted of `r trunc(min(meanDig))` to `r trunc(max(meanDig))` digits (*M* = `r round(mean(meanDig$NDigit),2)`, *SD* = `r round(sd(meanDig$NDigit),2)`). The first key question of this work, constituting the attempt to replicate the work of @wessel2021 and our first hypothesis, is the effect of an error on the conflict task on subsequent WM recall. The data show no significant deviation from a normal distribution.

**Figure 3: Accuracy and Response Time on Working Memory Task**

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
##########
# suppress 34 and 56 subject from base
base5 <- base5 %>%
  filter(!(Subject %in% c(36, 54)))

# t test for accuracy
result3 <- t.test(base5$Mean_Mem_correct, base5$Mean_Mem_erreur, paired=TRUE)

# Extraire les résultats du test
df3 <- result3$parameter  # Degrés de liberté
t_value3 <- result3$statistic  # Valeur t
p_value3 <- result3$p.value


# Calculer le coefficient de Cohen (Cohen's d)
cohen_d3<-cohens_d(t.test(base5$Mean_Mem_correct, base5$Mean_Mem_erreur)) %>% 
  select("Cohens_d") %>% 
  round(2)

# Effectuer le test t de Student pour temps de réponse
result4 <- t.test(base5$TR_Mem_Correct, base5$TR_Mem_Erreur, paired=TRUE)

# Extraire les résultats du test
df4 <- result4$parameter  # Degrés de liberté
t_value4 <- result4$statistic  # Valeur t
p_value4 <- result4$p.value

# Calculer le coefficient de Cohen (Cohen's d)
cohen_d4<-cohens_d(t.test(base5$TR_Mem_Correct, base5$TR_Mem_Erreur)) %>% 
  select("Cohens_d") %>%
  round(2)
```

We compared response accuracy of Working Memory recall in the two conditions (according to an error has been produced on conflict task or not) using paired-sample t-tests. Trials with an error on the conflict task are significantly less accurate than trials without (*t*(`r df3`) = `r round(t_value3,2)`, *p*`r format_p(p_value3)`, Cohen's *d* = `r cohen_d3$Cohens_d`). This effect is slightly larger than in the experiment 2 of Wessel et al. where the authors find a Cohen *d* = .32. Response accuracy between the correct and error conditions thus fell on average from `r round(mean(dataa$Accuracy.correct_trial,na.rm = TRUE),2)` to `r round(mean(dataa$Accuracy.error_trial,na.rm = TRUE),2)` respectively. This effect does not appear to be linked to an adjustment of the participants' response time/accuracy function, as response time of two conditions do not differ significantly (*t*(`r df4`) = `r round(t_value4,2)`, *p*`r format_p(p_value4)`, Cohen's *d* = `r cohen_d4$Cohens_d`). Action error commited during the delay period thus impaired subsequent working memory accuracy on the digit span recall. Our first hypothesis is thus corroborated by data, and ERIAM effect has been replicated.

## Hypothesis 2 testing

```{r data preparation H2, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
dfglm<-df %>% select(Subject, span, charge, eriam, WMC, Mean_Mem_erreur, moyNdigit, Mean_Mem_correct ) %>%

dfglm2 <- subset(dfglm, eriam != 0) #subset without 0value for eriam

# long format for data

# réordonner ordre de la variable condition

dfglmlong2$Accuracy_scaled <- scale(dfglmlong2$Accuracy, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)# centering
# dfglmlong2$Condition <- factor(dfglmlong2$Condition, levels = rev(levels(dfglmlong2$Condition)))

dfglmlong <- dfglmlong2 %>%
  group_by(charge, Condition, span) %>%

```

Then we want to know if this ERIAM effect is differently impacting high and low span group within our two cognitive load conditions. To test this hypothesis we fit a linear mixed model using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to assess for change in ERIAM level according to cognitive load and subject span group with the formula: $$eriam -> cognitive.load*span + (1|subject)$$

Mixed models allow us to deal with repeated measure within subject and non-independance of data. Proceding by model comparison, we start fitting a null model with formula and then we add predictors one by one: $$eriam -> 1 + (1|subject)$$ This first model allow us to check for intraclass correlation index (*ICC*).

```{r hypothesis 2 testing, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# eriam model for hypothesis testing / model comparison approach
#null model
modeleglm3 <- glmer(eriam_scaled ~ 1 + (1|Subject),
            family = gaussian,
            data = dfglmlong2)


# model 5 (1 predictor) has been fit later, name is not change to conserve further inlines
modeleglm5 <- glmer(eriam_scaled ~ span + (1|Subject),
            family = gaussian,
            data = dfglmlong2)
######## post analysis 
modeleglm55 <- glmer(eriam_scaled ~ span + charge+ (1|Subject),
            family = gaussian,
            data = dfglmlong2)
#######
modeleglm66 <- glmer(eriam_scaled ~ charge+ (1|Subject),
            family = gaussian,
            data = dfglmlong2)
#full model for hypothesis testing
modeleglm4 <- glmer(eriam_scaled ~ span * charge + (1|Subject),
            family = gaussian,
            data = dfglmlong2)



estimates_moderiam <- estimates(modeleglm3) # for ICC and design effect
compareglm3 <- model.comparison(modeleglm3, modeleglm66)
compareglm2 <- model.comparison(modeleglm3, modeleglm5)
report(modeleglm66)

# report(modeleglm4) #uncomment and run to see analysis of eriam model with predictor for hypothesis 2


```


We found an *ICC* = `r round(estimates_moderiam[["icc"]][["icc"]],2)`, indicating strong data dependency within subject. Design effect is telling us that we artificially increase the sample size by a `r round(estimates_moderiam[["icc"]][["design.effect"]],2)` factor not considering random effect. Mixed model is appropriated in this case. Compared to the *null model*, first model with span as a predictor do not yield significative improvement of fit to the data. *AIC* = `r round(compareglm3[["statistics"]][["aic"]][1],2)` for the *null model* and *AIC* = `r round(compareglm3[["statistics"]][["aic"]][2],2)` for the model with predictors while *BIC* = `r round(compareglm3[["statistics"]][["bic"]][1],2)` and `r round(compareglm3[["statistics"]][["bic"]][2],2)` respectively for *null model* and model with predictors. Finally, *Bayes Factor* do not really favor model, *Bf~10~* = `r round(compareglm3[["statistics"]][["bayes.factor"]][2],3)`, *p* = .098. Adding one predictor (cognitive load) to this model exhibits a significantly worse fit to the data compared to the null model. *AIC* = `r round(compareglm2[["statistics"]][["aic"]][1],2)` for the *null model* and *AIC* = `r round(compareglm2[["statistics"]][["aic"]][2],2)` for the model with predictors while *BIC* = `r round(compareglm2[["statistics"]][["bic"]][1],2)` and `r round(compareglm2[["statistics"]][["aic"]][2],2)` respectively for *null model* and model with span and cognitive load as predictors. Finally, *Bayes Factor* favored *null model*, *Bf~10~* = `r round(compareglm2[["statistics"]][["bayes.factor"]][2],3)`, *p* = .024. So we don't analyze the model with predictors (but you'll find results in the script). Thus our second hypothesis of a more pronounced ERIAM effect in *high span* group with increased cognitive load compared to *low span* group, with the analyses we carried out, is not supported by data. Nethertheless, we propose a visualization of these non-significant results in **Figure 4**.

**Figure 4: ERIAM effect according to cognitive load and group**

*None of the results yield significance*

## Exploratory part for in-depth understanding of the ERIAM effect

Going further in our understanding of the patern beyond the data we collect, we want to analyse accuracy on working memory recall as a more low level construct than ERIAM. We fit a new linear mixed model using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to assess for change in response accuracy on working memory task according to cognitive load, error on conflict task and subject span group with the formula: $$accuracy => cognitive.load*span*error + (1|subject)$$

In **Figure 5** you can find residuals distribution of the model.

**Figure 5: Mixed Model residuals**

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#### logistic regression
logistic <- data_grouped %>%
  transmute(
    Subject,
    flanker = ifelse(erreur_flanker == 0, "flanker_error", "flanker_correct"),
    Accuracy = ifelse(CollectResponse1.ACC == 0, "memory_error", "memory_correct"),
    Span = ifelse(moyNdigit < 7, "lowspan", "highspan"),
    LOAD = ifelse(Ndigit <= first_Ndigit, "moderate", "increased")
  )
# Accuracy in factor to fit the model
logistic <- logistic %>%
  mutate(Accuracy = factor(Accuracy, levels = c("memory_error", "memory_correct")))
logistic <- logistic %>%
  mutate(LOAD = factor(LOAD, levels = c("moderate", "increased")))

####### models definition
# Modèle Null (seulement effet aléatoire du sujet)
logistic_null <- glmer(Accuracy ~ 1 + (1 | Subject), data = logistic, family = binomial)

# Ajout de Span
logistic_1 <- glmer(Accuracy ~ Span + (1 | Subject), data = logistic, family = binomial)

# Ajout de LOAD
logistic_2 <- glmer(Accuracy ~ Span + LOAD + (1 | Subject), data = logistic, family = binomial)

# Ajout de flanker
logistic_3 <- glmer(Accuracy ~ Span + LOAD + flanker + (1 | Subject), data = logistic, family = binomial)

logistic_model <- glmer(Accuracy ~ Span * LOAD * flanker + (1 | Subject), 
               data = logistic, 
               family = binomial)

predictions <- logistic %>%
  mutate(predicted = predict(logistic_3, type = "response"))

predictions$Span <- factor(predictions$Span, levels = rev(levels(factor(predictions$Span))))

# Graphique des effets d'interaction
ggplot(predictions, aes(x = LOAD, y = predicted, color = flanker, group = flanker)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1), alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "binomial"), se = TRUE) + # Courbes de tendance

        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) # Centrer le titre


summary(logistic_3)

#### model comparison
model_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Null", "Span", "Span + LOAD", "Span + LOAD + Flanker", "Full Model"),
  AIC = c(AIC(logistic_null), AIC(logistic_1), AIC(logistic_2), AIC(logistic_3), AIC(logistic_model)),
  BIC = c(BIC(logistic_null), BIC(logistic_1), BIC(logistic_2), BIC(logistic_3), BIC(logistic_model))
)

# Affichage des résultats
```

```{r}
# Charger les bibliothèques nécessaires
library(lme4)
library(BayesFactor)
library(dplyr)

# Créer le dataframe logistic
logistic <- data_grouped %>%
  transmute(
    Subject,
    flanker = ifelse(erreur_flanker == 0, "flanker_error", "flanker_correct"),
    Accuracy = ifelse(CollectResponse1.ACC == 0, "memory_error", "memory_correct"),
    Span = ifelse(moyNdigit < 7, "lowspan", "highspan"),
    LOAD = ifelse(Ndigit <= first_Ndigit, "moderate", "increased")
  )

# Charger les packages nécessaires
library(brms)
library(loo)

# Création des modèles Bayésiens avec save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)

# 1. Modèle nul (intercept seulement)
model_null_bayes <- brm(Accuracy ~ 1 + (1 | Subject), 
                        data = logistic, 
                        family = bernoulli(), 
                        chains = 4, iter = 2000, 
                        save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE))

# 2. Modèle avec Span seul
model_1_bayes <- brm(Accuracy ~ Span + (1 | Subject), 
                      data = logistic, 
                      family = bernoulli(), 
                      chains = 4, iter = 2000, 
                      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE))

# 3. Modèle avec Span + LOAD
model_2_bayes <- brm(Accuracy ~ Span + LOAD + (1 | Subject), 
                      data = logistic, 
                      family = bernoulli(), 
                      chains = 4, iter = 2000, 
                      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE))

# 4. Modèle avec Span + LOAD + flanker
model_3_bayes <- brm(Accuracy ~ Span + LOAD + flanker + (1 | Subject), 
                      data = logistic, 
                      family = bernoulli(), 
                      chains = 4, iter = 2000, 
                      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE))

# 5. Modèle avec interaction Span * LOAD
model_4_bayes <- brm(Accuracy ~ Span * LOAD + flanker + (1 | Subject), 
                      data = logistic, 
                      family = bernoulli(), 
                      chains = 4, iter = 2000, 
                      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE))

# 6. Modèle complet avec toutes les interactions (Span * LOAD * flanker)
model_full_bayes <- brm(Accuracy ~ Span * LOAD * flanker + (1 | Subject), 
                         data = logistic, 
                         family = bernoulli(), 
                         chains = 4, iter = 2000, 
                         save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE))

# Comparaison des modèles avec LOO, AIC et BIC
loo_null <- loo(model_null_bayes)
loo_1 <- loo(model_1_bayes)
loo_2 <- loo(model_2_bayes)
loo_3 <- loo(model_3_bayes)
loo_4 <- loo(model_4_bayes)
loo_full <- loo(model_full_bayes)

# Comparer les modèles avec loo_compare()
model_comparison <- loo_compare(loo_null, loo_1, loo_2, loo_3, loo_4, loo_full)

# Afficher les résultats
print(model_comparison)

# Calcul des Facteurs de Bayes pour comparer les modèles
bf_1 <- bayes_factor(model_null_bayes, model_1_bayes)
bf_2 <- bayes_factor(model_1_bayes, model_2_bayes)
bf_3 <- bayes_factor(model_2_bayes, model_3_bayes)
bf_4 <- bayes_factor(model_3_bayes, model_4_bayes)
bf_full <- bayes_factor(model_4_bayes, model_full_bayes)

# Regrouper les résultats des facteurs de Bayes dans un tableau
bf_results <- data.frame(
  Model_Comparison = c("Null vs Span", "Span vs Span+LOAD", "Span+LOAD vs Span+LOAD+flanker",
                       "Span*LOAD vs Span*LOAD+flanker", "Full Model"),
  Bayes_Factor = c(bf_1$bf, bf_2$bf, bf_3$bf, bf_4$bf, bf_full$bf)
)

print(bf_results)

########## visualisation

# Prédictions du modèle bayésien
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)

# Prédictions du modèle bayésien sans messages d'avertissement
predictions_bayes <- logistic %>%
  mutate(predicted = fitted(model_full_bayes, scale = "response", silent = TRUE)[, "Estimate"])

# Graphique des effets d'interaction basé sur model_full_bayes
ggplot(predictions_bayes, aes(x = LOAD, y = predicted, color = flanker, group = flanker)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1), alpha = 0.5) +  # Points avec jitter
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", se = TRUE) +  # Courbes de tendance avec intervalle de confiance
  facet_wrap(~ Span) +  # Séparation selon Span
  labs(x = "Cognitive Load",
       y = "Predicted Accuracy (Bayesian Model)",
       color = "Flanker Response") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("flanker_correct" = "lightgreen", "flanker_error" = "#F78B8B")) +  # Couleurs personnalisées
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(text = element_text(family = "Times New Roman"),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))  # Centrer le titre

```

Again, *ICC* = `r round(estimates_modnull[["icc"]][["icc"]],2)`, indicates strong data dependency within subject and design effect = `r round(estimates_modnull[["icc"]][["design.effect"]],2)`. Model REML is `r round(modelLLM_summary[["AICtab"]],2)`. Compared to the *null model*, the model with predictors exhibits a significantly improved fit to the data. *AIC* = `r round(compareglm[["statistics"]][["aic"]][1],2)` for the *null model* and *AIC* = `r round(compareglm[["statistics"]][["aic"]][2],2)` for the model with predictors while *BIC* = `r round(compareglm[["statistics"]][["bic"]][1],2)` and `r round(compareglm[["statistics"]][["aic"]][2],2)` respectively for *null model* and model with predictors. Finally, *Bayes Factor* overwhelmingly favored model with predictors, *Bf~10~* = `r format(compareglm[["statistics"]][["bayes.factor"]][2], scientific = TRUE, digits = 2)`, *p* \< .001. Residuals visually do not differ from a normal distribution. The model's total explanatory power is substantial (conditional *R^2^* = 0.77) and the part related to the fixed effects alone (marginal *R^2^*) is of 0.29. The model's intercept, corresponding to span = lowspan, charge = moderate and Condition = Correct, is at `r round(estimates_modglm[["fixed"]][["(Intercept)"]],2)` (95% CI \[`r round(modelglmconfint[3,1],2)`, `r round(modelglmconfint[3,2],2)`\], *t*(192) = 5.96, *p* \< .001). Accuracy values are standardized, hereafter we only report standardized *beta* coefficients for better visibility. Within this model:

-   The effect of span \[highspan\] is statistically significant and negative, *t*(192) = -4.57, *p* \< .001; *Std. beta* = -1.11, 95% CI \[-1.58, -0.63\])
-   The effect of charge \[increased\] is statistically significant and negative, *t*(192) = -7.15, *p* \< .001; *Std. beta* = -1.08, 95% CI \[-1.38, -0.78\])
-   The effect of Condition \[Error\] is statistically significant and negative, *t*(192) = -3.60, *p* \< .001; *Std. beta* = -0.54, 95% CI \[-0.83, -0.24\])
-   The effect of span \[highspan\] × charge \[increased\] is statistically significant and positive, *t*(192) = 2.24, *p* = 0.026; *Std. beta* = 0.46, 95% CI \[0.06, 0.87\])
-   The effect of span \[highspan\] × Condition \[Error\] is statistically non-significant and positive, *t*(192) = 1.56, p = 0.122; *Std. beta* = 0.30, 95% CI \[-0.08, 0.69\])
-   The effect of charge \[increased\] × Condition \[Error\] is statistically non-significant and positive, *t*(192) = 1.08, p = 0.279; *Std. beta* = 0.23, 95% CI \[-0.19, 0.65\])
-   The effect of (span \[highspan\] × charge \[increased\]) × Condition \[Error\] is statistically non-significant and negative, *t*(192) = -0.80, *p* = 0.426; *Std. beta* = -0.23, 95% CI \[-0.80, 0.34\]) 95% Confidence Intervals (CIs) and p-values were computed using a Wald t-distribution approximation.

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Create a data frame with the results
resultsglm <- data.frame(
  Effect = c("span [highspan]", "charge [increased]", "Condition [Error]",
             "span [highspan] × charge [increased]", 
             "span [highspan] × Condition [Error]", 
             "charge [increased] × Condition [Error]", 
             "(span [highspan] × charge [increased]) × Condition [Error]"),
  Test = c("t(192) = -4.57, p < .001", "t(192) = -7.15, p < .001", "t(192) = -3.60, p < .001",
           "t(192) = 2.24, p = 0.026", "t(192) = 1.56, p = 0.122", 
           "t(192) = 1.08, p = 0.279", "t(192) = -0.80, p = 0.426"),
  `Std. beta` = c("-1.11", "-1.08", "-0.54", "0.46", "0.30", "0.23", "-0.23"),
  `95% CI` = c("[-1.58, -0.63]", "[-1.38, -0.78]", "[-0.83, -0.24]", "[0.06, 0.87]",
               "[-0.08, 0.69]", "[-0.19, 0.65]", "[-0.80, 0.34]")
)

# Print the results in APA format
apa_table(resultsglm, caption = "Summary of mixed model on accuracy",placement ="h",font_size = "small", resize_mode = "resize_columns", note = "For every effect tested, t test and pvalue, standardized beta coefficient and 95% CI are mentioned")
```

**Figure 6** represent response accuracy according to group span (high and low span) and working memory load (moderate and increased load). Following our model results, increasing the cognitive load has a significant negative effect on digit span accuracy. Then, error made on the conflict task also significantly impair accuracy, arguing again for the ERIAM effect. Finally, increasing cognitive load in *high span* does not impact accuracy level as in *low span* group.

**Figure 6: Accuracy on Working Memory task**

## Hypothesis 3 testing

As mentioned in our preregistration [@brochet2022], we then check for correlation between ERIAM and WMC as in @wessel2021b. In **Table 3** are represented ERIAM and correlation ERIAM/WMC in both groups of participants within level of cognitive load. Remember that our alpha threshold for significance is set to .029 due to Pocock correction. With this precision, we see that ERIAM effect seems to be significant only in *high span*/*increased load* and *low span*/*moderate load*, and correlation ERIAM/WMC is significant in low span group in increased load condition. Our third hypothesis cannot be corroborated by data we collected. We cannot say that ERIAM/WMC correlation significantly increase in high span group within cognitive load as linear link does not yield significativity. Nethertheless, in low span group, the linear relation between ERIAM/WMC become significant as cognitive load increase.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, paged.print=TRUE}
df9 <- rbind(df5, df6, df7, df8)  # Combine all dataframes into one
df9 <- df9[df9$eriam != 0 & !is.na(df9$eriam), ]


eriam_summary <- df9 %>%
  group_by(span, charge) %>%
  summarize(
    ERIAM = round(mean(eriam, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    n = sum(!is.na(eriam)),  # Nombre de valeurs non NA pour calculer SE
    SE = round(sd(eriam, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n), 2),  # Erreur standard (SE)
    pvalue = round(t.test(eriam)$p.value, 3)  # Test t pour p-value
  )



cor_summary <- df9 %>%
  group_by(span, charge) %>%
  summarize(ERIAM_WMC = round(cor(eriam, WMC, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), 2),
            p = format_p(cor.test(eriam, WMC, method = "spearman")$p.value))

WMC_summary <- df9 %>%
  group_by(span, charge) %>%  
  summarise(
    Mean_WMC = round(mean(WMC, na.rm = TRUE), 2),  # Moyenne de WMC
    n_WMC = sum(!is.na(WMC)),  # Nombre de valeurs non NA
    se_WMC = ifelse(n_WMC > 1, round(sd(WMC, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n_WMC), 2), NA),  # Écart-type sur WMC
    IC_95 = ifelse(!is.na(se_WMC), 
                   paste0("[", round(Mean_WMC - 1.96 * se_WMC, 2), ", ", round(Mean_WMC + 1.96 * se_WMC, 2), "]"), 
                   "[NA, NA]")
  )



# Fusionner eriam_summary et cor_summary d'abord
merged_summary <- merge(eriam_summary, cor_summary, by = c("span", "charge"))

# Puis fusionner avec WMC_summary
merged_summary <- merge(merged_summary, WMC_summary, by = c("span", "charge"))
```

```{r}
library(MASS)  # Pour la génération de variables aléatoires multinormales
library(dplyr) # Pour la manipulation des données

# # Fonction de simulation
Simulation <- function(nRep, nSub, means, rSample, rS, rTol) {
  sigma <- matrix(c(1, rSample * sqrt(rS[2] / rS[1]),
                    rSample * sqrt(rS[2] / rS[1]), rS[2] / rS[1]),
                  nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
   
  d <- mvrnorm(n = nSub, mu = means / rS[1], Sigma = sigma)

  x <- d[, 1] - d[, 2]  # ERIAM
  y <- (d[, 1] + d[, 2]) / 2  # WMC

  r <- numeric(nRep)

  for (i in 1:nRep) {
    idx <- sample(1:nSub, nSub, replace = TRUE)
    x1 <- x[idx]
    y1 <- y[idx]
    r[i] <- cor(x1, y1)
  }

  return(list(r = r))
}

# Regrouper par sujet et ne conserver qu'une seule ligne par sujet
df_unique <- dfcorallreg %>% 
  group_by(Subject) %>% 
  summarise(
    Mean_Mem_erreur = mean(Mean_Mem_erreur, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean_Mem_correct = mean(Mean_Mem_correct, na.rm = TRUE),
    NDigit = mean(moyNdigit, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>% 
  na.omit()
df_unique <- df_unique %>% filter(eriam != 0)
# Calcul des nouvelles variables
eriam <- df_unique$Mean_Mem_correct - df_unique$Mean_Mem_erreur  # ERIAM
WMC <- (df_unique$Mean_Mem_correct + df_unique$Mean_Mem_erreur) / 2  # WMC
NDigit <- df_unique$NDigit

# Groupes Low Span et High Span
low_span <- df_unique$NDigit < 7
high_span <- df_unique$NDigit >= 7

# Moyennes et variances
means <- c(mean(eriam), mean(WMC))
rS <- c(var(eriam), var(WMC))
rTol <- 0.01

# Nombre de simulations
nSimulations <- 50000
nSub <- length(eriam)

# Corrélation empirique
cor_empirical <- cor(eriam, WMC, method = "spearman")

# Simulation pour l'ensemble des sujets
resultats <- Simulation(nRep = nSimulations, nSub = nSub, means = means,
                        rSample = cor_empirical, rS = rS, rTol = rTol)

p_value_empirical <- mean(resultats$r >= cor_empirical)

# Simulation pour Low Span
cor_empirical_low <- cor(eriam[low_span], WMC[low_span])
resultats_low <- Simulation(nRep = nSimulations, nSub = sum(low_span), means = means,
                            rSample = cor_empirical_low, rS = rS, rTol = rTol)
p_value_empirical_low <- mean(resultats_low$r >= cor_empirical_low)

# Simulation pour High Span
cor_empirical_high <- cor(eriam[high_span], WMC[high_span])
resultats_high <- Simulation(nRep = nSimulations, nSub = sum(high_span), means = means,
                             rSample = cor_empirical_high, rS = rS, rTol = rTol)
p_value_empirical_high <- mean(resultats_high$r >= cor_empirical_high)

# Affichage des résultats
cat("Corrélation empirique (ensemble) :", round(cor_empirical, 4), "\n")
cat("P-value empirique (ensemble) :", round(p_value_empirical, 4), "\n")
cat("Corrélation empirique (Low Span) :", round(cor_empirical_low, 4), "\n")
cat("P-value empirique (Low Span) :", round(p_value_empirical_low, 4), "\n")
cat("Corrélation empirique (High Span) :", round(cor_empirical_high, 4), "\n")
cat("P-value empirique (High Span) :", round(p_value_empirical_high, 4), "\n")

# Graphique de distribution des corrélations simulées
x_min <- floor(min(c(resultats$r, resultats_low$r, resultats_high$r, cor_empirical, cor_empirical_low, cor_empirical_high)) / 0.1) * 0.1
x_max <- ceiling(max(c(resultats$r, resultats_low$r, resultats_high$r, cor_empirical, cor_empirical_low, cor_empirical_high)) / 0.1) * 0.1

dens <- density(resultats$r)
plot(dens, main = NULL,
     xlab = "Correlation", col = "lightgreen", lwd = 2,
     xlim = c(x_min, x_max), bty = "n")
polygon(dens, col = "lightgreen", border = NA)

# dens_low <- density(resultats_low$r)
# lines(dens_low, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
# polygon(dens_low, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.2), border = NA)
# 
# dens_high <- density(resultats_high$r)
# lines(dens_high, col = "red", lwd = 2)
# polygon(dens_high, col = rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.2), border = NA)

abline(v = cor_empirical, col = "lightgreen", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
# abline(v = cor_empirical_low, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
# abline(v = cor_empirical_high, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

axis(1, at = seq(x_min, x_max, by = 0.2))

p_value_apa <- ifelse(p_value_empirical < 0.001, "p < .001", paste("p = ", round(p_value_empirical, 3)))
# p_value_apa_low <- ifelse(p_value_empirical_low < 0.001, "p < .001", paste("p = ", round(p_value_empirical_low, 3)))

#bootstrap for 95%CI
spearman_cor <- function(data, indices) {
  d <- data[indices, ]
  return(cor(d$eriam, d$WMC, method = "spearman"))
}

# Prepare data

# Print results

cat("95% Confidence Interval:", ci$percent[4], "-", ci$percent[5], "\n")

# Créer une fonction pour calculer les lignes de régression pour chaque tau
predictions <- function(tau, rq_model, data) {
  intercept <- coef(rq_model)[1, tau]
  slope <- coef(rq_model)[2, tau]
  return(intercept + slope * data$eriam)
}
```

## Second exploratory part

We finally observed the link between WMC and ERIAM effect for the whole group in the same way as @wessel2021 propose in their study. In the opposite direction to the replicated study, we observe a positive correlation between WM capacities and ERIAM effect, *r*(`r dfcorall$df`) = `r round(dfcorall$ERIAM_WMC,2)`. This correlation is significant for the whole group, *F*(1, `r dfcorall$df`) = `r round(dfcorall$f_value,2)`, *p* `r format_p(dfcorall$p)` . For the Low Span group, the link between WM capacities and ERIAM effect is not significant *r*(`r dfcorlow$df`) = `r round(dfcorlow$ERIAM_WMC,2)`, *F*(1,`r dfcorlow$df`) = `r round(dfcorlow$f_value,2)`, *p* `r format_p(dfcorlow$p)`. Concerning High Span group, we observe a trend for positive linear relationship *r*(`r dfcorhigh$df`) = `r round(dfcorhigh$ERIAM_WMC,2)`, *F*(1,`r dfcorhigh$df`) = `r round(dfcorhigh$f_value,2)`, *p* `r format_p(dfcorhigh$p)` which does not reach .029 threshold of significance. **Figures 7, 8 and 9** show graphic representation of linear relationships observed at group level (**Figure 7**), in low-span (**Figure 8**) and high-span (**Figure 9**) groups. In **Table 4** you can find means and standard errors values for ERIAM and WMC within each span group. It is worth noting that WMC is larger for the lowspan group than for the highspan group, probably due to our task complexity and the way we split participants into span groups.
