# Discussion

To test our first hypothesis, we observed the effect of a motor error on Working Memory maintenance (ERIAM), by carrying out a replication/extension of experiment 2 by @wessel2021. We succeeded in replicating this effect for the whole group. When participants made a mistake on the flanker task, memory recall was significantly impaired. The authors mention that in experiments where they use an arrow flanker task, ERIAM effect was probably facilitated by the similarity of the processes involved in the response modalities of the two parts of the task, both of which are dichotomous. Through different operationalization proposed in our study (recall of the digit rather than recognition) we show that ERIAM effect is also present when two parts of the task do not rely on the same response keys. Moreover, as our participants were not stressed by short response time on Working Memory task, ERIAM is still observable at longer delay period after error is made, probably signifying loss of memory trace.

To explain these results, going back to Adaptive Orienting Theory (AOT) [@wessel2017] is useful. AOT predicts that errors lead to an impairment of cognitive processes in progress. Memory tasks involve encoding, storage (with rehearsal for WM) and retrievial of information. We probably can exclude here effect of the error on retrievial process because our operationalisation of recall was not time-limited and should have normally enabled participants to perform equally in both conditions (error or correct). Nethertheless, we cannot conclude which of the other two processes (encoding or storage) is impacted by the effect of the error. If we assume that encoding is done before the conflict task starts, probably error compete with rehearsal processes in Working Memory, as it diverts limited attentional ressources also in use for Working Memory maintenance [@barrouillet2020].

@oberauer2019 reminds us that of "*theoretical options for spelling out the idea of WM as relying on an attentional resource*", that of a shared resource for storage and processing has received the most theoretical support. In our case and on the basis of functional theories of PES, error detection engage deployment of cognitive control [@botvinick2001] to be monitored. As this process take place, processing resource are focused on error monitoring and and take up some of the common attentional resources allocated to information storage in working memory. This needs to be disentangled by proposing other protocols specifically studying these constructs.

Concerning our second hypothesis of a differential impact of increased cognitive load in the two High and Low Span groups, we implemented a mixed model using REML handling non independant data to predict ERIAM. Neither cognitive load nor group span are good predictors of ERIAM effect in our model. Proceding by model comparison and a one by one factor incremental method, neither model reach better fit to the data than null model. We believe in this case that ERIAM is already a highly transformed summary of data (𝛅 between mean correct and mean error accuracy). Our model cannot explain a significantly sufficient part of variance of ERIAM when controling for span group nor cognitive load. This may be because of insufficient statistical power due to low sample size (e.g. low span group in this case has a 20 participants sample). But it may also be a consequence of mixed model and all variance falling into random factor. This conclusion is far from being trustworthy in our study and need further investigation.

Next we proposed an exploratory part trying to predict accuracy with group span, cognitive load and error made on conflict task. Accuracy is a lower-leveled construct than ERIAM. While turning back to this level our goal is to have a simplified understanding of predictors and data. This time, model with predictors is significantly better fitted to our data than null model. With this model we find that all simple predictors' effect are significant. Error made on conflict task (ERIAM effect), cognitive load and High span group all have a significant negative effect on accuracy. Interestingly, interaction of group span and cognitive load is significant too. The combination of High span group and increased cognitive load have a significant positive effect on accuracy. More precisely (see **Figure 6**), we can see that accuracy is less impaired by the increase of cognitive load in High span than in Low span group. It is possible that High span participants are more engaged in task when cognitive load increase and thus perform better.

To say more about simple effects of predictors within this model, first we can see that error factor has a significant negative effect on accuracy. That doesn't come as much of a surprise because it reflects ERIAM effect already found in hypothesis 1 testing. This time however, we find this fixed effect of error while controling for random effect. Then, High span group has a lower accuracy level than low span group. This probably comes from our experimental design that categorizes High and Low span groups according to the number of digits reached in the empanel at the end of the training phase. For High span participants, it may be that trials have been more challenging and their performance significantly lower than Low span participants. Finally, cognitive load has a detrimental effect on accuracy for all participants. As we can imagine, adding one digit to a span already calibrated on your own capacities is likely to make the task even more complex. This effect of cognitive load is nevertheless modified by an interaction effect with the group of participants.

Effect of interaction between span group and cognitive load on accuracy is significant and positive (see **Figure 6**). We can see on the graph that when cognitive load increase, High span individuals are less impacted than Low span. Their accuracy on working memory task is less impaired than these of Low span when cognitive load increase. Even if our predictions of hypothesis 2 concerning ERIAM effect do not raise significativity, it can be interesting here to compare visual observations of increasing cognitive load on ERIAM against accuracy. As proposed by @thomassin2015, High span individuals have more complex strategies that lead to both better performance and greater susceptibility to an increase in cognitive load. It seems that our data go in this way. ERIAM effect is visually as important in both conditions of load for High span group, which can be related to the performance susceptibility part of the High span group. On the other way, their more complex strategies lead to a more stable accuracy performance within the two cognitive load conditions. But this is open to caution, as we are dealing in this part with an exploratory approach and, what's more, using results that are not significant.

Our third hypothesis has not be corroborated by data. Correlation between ERIAM and WMC, when controling for group span and cognitive load, only reach significance in Low span group and increased cognitive load condition. No particular patern in our data is observed, probably because in this part of our study our analysis rely on complex constructs (ERIAM and WMC are highly transformed data) and need more power (increased sample size) to reach significance. On this part of our work, it seems we cannot go further with our sample size. Here is a limit of our study.

Finally, we conducted linear regression analyses to test the link between WMC and the ERIAM effect for the whole group. We observed a positive and significant link between WMC and ERIAM effect. These results are in the opposite direction to those obtained by @wessel2021, who find a negative correlation and explained that "*ERIAM most affected subjects for whom the WM aspect of the task was more challenging.*" In our study, ERIAM effect increases as WMC increases for the whole group. Splitting our sample in High and Low span groups, we can observed that correlation ERIAM/WMC does not reach our alpha level (Pocock corrected for one interim analysis). Nethertheless, a trend of a positive linear relationship is observed in High span group. However, as we can see in **Table 4**, this particular results are probably due to our span group splitting, as lowspan have better average WMC than highspan. With this in mind, we can better understand the correlation between ERIAM and WMC.

Highspan participants have a less impaired performance on digits span recall when they commited an error on flanker task (lower ERIAM levels). Nethertheless, their WMC is lower than lowspan group probably because they have reached high levels of task complexity. On the other hand, lowspan participants are more proned to ERIAM. This results drive the correlation between ERIAM and WMC in our sample, as higher WMC are reached by lowspan participants probably because of less complexity of the task in this group. As @wessel2021 say, "*The likely explanation for this finding is that subjects with a lower overall WM accuracy maintain less stable WM representations, which are then more susceptible to the impairing effects of errors*." In our data, this lower "*WM accuracy"* are observed for highspan individuals, what probably leads to our positive relationship between ERIAM and WMC.

According to Lavie (2010), "*The ability to focus attention \[...\] deteriorates under conditions of high load on cognitive control processes such as working memory.*" In our study we find data in the direction of this theoretical prediction as accuracy levels on Working Memory task seem to decrease as we increase cognitive load (see exploratory part **2.3**). Interestingly, Lavie's theory of load encompass both the effects of perceptual and cognitive loads. While a high perceptual load reduces the processing of irrelevant stimuli, a high cognitive load increases it. Turning back to PEA functional and non-functional explanations, it is commonly accepted that error is an irrelevant stimulus to the task at hand. Error diverts attention and engage or not (depending on theory) further processing to regain maximum performance levels.

ERIAM effect is only significant in lowspan group in the moderate cognitive load condition and in highspan group in the increased load condition (**Table 3**). Refering to Lavie's load theory, we can presume that for lowspan participants the increased cognitive load condition exceeds their capacities. Lowspan in this condition probably withdraw their cognitive control on task at hand, probably explaining why ERIAM is not found in this group under this load condition. Error has probably been filtered at a perceptual level and so does not engage any further processing leading to ERIAM. On the other hand, the opposite pattern is observed for highspan participants. Highspan within moderate cognitive load condition probably do not engage further processing on flanker task and treat it at a perceptual level, focusing only on digit span part of the task (but we can see a non-significant trend for ERIAM even in this condition). When cognitive load is increased however ERIAM becomes significant in this group. This may be because highspan are more motivated by task and treat all stimuli at a cognitive level. This can lead to increasing interference of error events as Lavie postulated.

# Conclusion

In conclusion, our study provides significant insights into the relationship between motor errors and Working Memory maintenance (ERIAM), as well as the influence of cognitive load and individual differences in working memory capacity. Firstly, we successfully replicated previous findings demonstrating that motor errors impair memory recall, extending this effect to tasks with different response modalities, indicating a broader applicability of ERIAM across task variations. Our results align with Adaptive Orienting Theory, suggesting that error detection diverts attentional resources from memory maintenance processes, particularly rehearsal in Working Memory. However, the exact impact on encoding versus storage remains inconclusive and warrants further investigation.

Secondly, while our hypotheses regarding differential effects of cognitive load and working memory capacity on ERIAM were not fully supported, our exploratory analysis revealed intriguing patterns. High-span individuals exhibited more stable accuracy under increased cognitive load compared to low-span individuals, possibly due to their engagement in more complex strategies. This suggests that individual differences in working memory capacity may modulate the impact of cognitive load on task performance.

Additionally, our study highlights the intricate interplay between cognitive load, error processing, and working memory capacity. High cognitive load conditions seemed to exacerbate the ERIAM effect, particularly in high-span individuals, potentially due to increased interference from error events. Conversely, low-span individuals may disengage cognitive control under high load conditions, leading to reduced susceptibility to ERIAM.

Moreover, our findings regarding the correlation between ERIAM and Working Memory Capacity (WMC) diverged from previous research, with a positive relationship observed in our study. This discrepancy may be attributed to differences in task complexity and individual cognitive strategies. High-span individuals exhibited lower ERIAM levels but also lower WMC, possibly indicating a ceiling effect due to task complexity for this group.

Overall, our study contributes to the understanding of how motor errors impact working memory maintenance, shedding light on the moderating roles of cognitive load and individual differences in working memory capacity. Future research should further elucidate the underlying mechanisms of ERIAM and its implications for cognitive control processes. Additionally, investigations into the interaction between error processing, cognitive load, and individual cognitive characteristics could provide valuable insights into optimizing task performance and cognitive resource allocation.
